newsitem.title: United Nations: Annan wins unofficial poll for U.N. secretary-general.
newsitem.headline: Annan wins unofficial poll for U.N. secretary-general.

text.p: Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations, won the unanimous support of Security Council members on Friday in an unofficial poll for U.N. secretary-general after France dropped a veto threat.

"We have consensus in the council to recommend to the General Assembly that the next secretary-general should be Mr. Kofi Annan," British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston said. "This is a good result for Africa and for the U.N. organisation," he told reporters, paying tribute to the incumbent secretary-general, Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

The 74-year-old Boutros-Ghali, a veteran Egyptian diplomat, had hoped for a second five-year term beginning on Jan. 1 but was blocked by a United States veto in an official council vote on Nov. 19 in which he was the only candidate.

Washington insists the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms and expended considerable diplomatic effort, capital and goodwill in blocking Boutros-Ghali, who suspended his candidacy earlier this month.

Annan's unofficial victory in the council's latest "straw" vote must be ratified at a formal council meeting, scheduled for 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT). The council's official nominee for secretary-general will then be passed on to the 185-member General Assembly, which makes the formal appointment.

"The secretary-general warmly congratulates Mr. Kofi Annan of Ghana on receiving the recommendation of the Security Council to become the next secretary-general," a statement issued by Boutros-Ghali's spokeswoman said.

"The secretary-general is pleased that the decision was unanimous and is especially gratified that Africa has been able to maintain the office of secretary-general for a second five-year term, the objective which the secretary-general has sought throughout these recent months."

The statement said Boutros-Ghali had worked closely with Annan "and wishes him every success." Boutros-Ghali also expressed thanks for the support he had received over the past five years by the members and peoples of the United Nations.
U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said she was pleased Annan would become the new secretary-general. "It has been a good and successful process and I am very pleased," she said.
She also complimented Boutros-Ghali on "the hard work he has performed during his term," saying "he has made his mark in history."
After Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4, Annan, from English-speaking Ghana, and three other African candidates from French-speaking countries entered the race.

France, which had supported the re-election of the Sorbonne-educated Boutros-Ghali, was angered by the U.S. veto. But it switched its support to candidates from Francophone Africa and voted against Annan in each of seven unofficial rounds of balloting held since Tuesday, signifying a veto once a formal vote was scheduled.
The council's five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- all have a veto.

In the seventh round of polling on Thursday, Annan obtained the backing of 14 of the council's 15 members. His closest rival had been Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and the 1994-95 U.N. General Assembly president.
Essy got seven votes on Thursday but those opposing him included two permanent members, the United States and Britain.

The two other candidates, who consistently fell far short of the minimum of nine votes needed, were Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah, a former foreign minister of Mauritania and former U.N. envoy for Burundi; and Hamid Algabid, a former prime minister of Niger and currently secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.

Had France persisted in opposing Annan, the race for secretary-general could have been thrown open to candidates from other continents. African candidates had been given priority so far on grounds that if Boutros-Ghali was denied the second term enjoyed by his predecessors, his successor should at least also come from an African country.
Previous U.N. secretaries-general were Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, Kurt Waldheim of Austria, U Thant of Burma, Dag Hammarskjoeld of Sweden and Trygve Lie of Norway.
